planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost on a heat mat, as germination is slow; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60F.

directions: A UK-bred superhot related to the Trinidad 7 Pot family, briefly holding a Guinness World Record for hottest chile in early 2011 before being displaced by other Trinidad Scorpion strains. Pods are wrinkled and habanero-shaped, ripening from green to deep red, with heat exceeding one million Scoville units. Give plants a long, warm season and full sun, and wear gloves when handling ripe fruit. Best grown in large containers or greenhouses outside tropical climates to accommodate its extended maturity time.

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil once nights are reliably above 60F.

directions: A rare Trinidadian 7 Pot strain that ripens to a pale ivory-white rather than the usual red or brown, with wrinkled habanero-shaped pods and a sweet, fruity flavor with hints of celery. Heat is in the superhot range, commonly reported above one million Scoville units. Plants are tall and vigorous with creamy yellow flowers and benefit from staking in windy sites. Harvest once pods fully whiten for the mildest flavor-to-heat balance this strain offers.

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil and nights are reliably warm.

directions: Named for the Trinidadian town of Chaguanas, this superhot pod is more elongated and pimpled than a typical 7 Pot, ripening from green to bright red. Heat runs 800,000 to 1,000,000 Scoville units with a notably fruity flavor alongside the characteristic 7 Pot heat. Give plants a long warm season, full sun, and even moisture to avoid blossom drop. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest once fully colored for peak flavor.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed.

directions: A commercially bred superhot introduced to the UK market in 2019 and selected for faster, more reliable production than most Capsicum chinense superhots. Compact, upright plants bear small, roughly 2-inch pods that ripen quickly and pack around 1.3 million Scoville units of heat. The shorter 75-to-95-day maturity window makes it more practical for cooler or shorter-season gardens than many superhot types. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and stake lightly if plants become top-heavy with fruit.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed and nights stay above 55F.

directions: An Indian heirloom-type eggplant producing strikingly long, slender fruit with marbled green-and-purple skin that can reach two feet or more under good growing conditions. Flesh is tender and mild-flavored, well suited to roasting, frying, or traditional curries and stir-fries. Plants are vigorous and productive over a long harvest season; stake tall fruiting branches to keep elongated pods off the ground. Harvest while skin is still glossy for the best texture, as overripe fruit turns dull and develops seeds.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights are reliably above 55F.

directions: A Japanese heirloom producing extra-long, slender dark purple fruit with a velvety, nutty flavor that stays sweet and never bitter even as pods size up. Tender skin allows the fruit to be eaten raw, grilled, or sauteed without peeling. Plants show good tolerance for summer heat and humidity, making this a reliable choice for warm climates. Harvest regularly to keep the glossy skin tight and encourage continued fruit set.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed.

directions: An East China heirloom named for its remarkably thin, string-like pods, which grow 10 to 15 inches long with lavender-violet skin over white, buttery flesh. The thin skin needs no peeling and the fruit is tender enough to eat raw in salads when picked young. Plants are high-yielding and quick to mature, performing well in both greenhouse and outdoor culture in warm climates. Pick young and often, as older fruit can toughen and develop seeds.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay reliably above 55F.

directions: A Japanese-type F1 hybrid eggplant bearing long, slender, glossy black fruit with a purple calyx on an upright, medium-tall plant. It is notably early to mature compared to other Asian eggplant types, suiting both open-field and greenhouse production. Flesh is tender with a mild flavor typical of slender Asian types, good for stir-fries, grilling, or tempura. Harvest while the skin retains its deep sheen, since dulling skin signals overripe fruit.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed.

directions: An open-pollinated Japanese eggplant named for the city of Kurume in Fukuoka Prefecture, bearing shiny, deep purple-black fruit 9 to 10 inches long on black stems with a purple calyx. The flavor is mild and the flesh notably soft, making it a favorite for tempura and pickling as well as stir-frying and braising. It is vigorous and one of the earliest Japanese types to mature. Harvest while fruit is still glossy and firm for the best texture.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed and soil is warm.

directions: A Thai specialty eggplant producing small, round, pale-green fruit about 1.5 to 2 inches across with distinct dark-green striping and slight ribbing. Flesh is mild and faintly sweet, popular raw or cooked in Thai, Indian, and Vietnamese curries. Plants are well-branched and somewhat less vigorous than standard round Thai types, so give consistent water and fertility. Pick young while pale green for the mildest flavor, as pods yellow and toughen with age.
